lede: A stratified sample is a small copy of a group that keeps its shape. A school picking 60 pupils for a survey takes more from Year 11 than from Year 8 if Year 11 is bigger, in exactly the same proportion. The second half of this topic estimates a population you could never count.
can: Work out how many each group contributes to a sample.
Round a share to a whole person and check the total.
Work backwards to a sample size or a population figure.

md: A sample is meant to stand in for the whole group, so it ought to look like the whole group. If a fifth of the population is in Year 8, a fifth of the sample should be too. That is all stratification is: each group's share of the sample is its share of the population, written as a fraction and multiplied by the size of the sample.

prompt: In a stratified sample, how much of the sample does each group get?
options: The same share it has of the population
An equal number from every group
answer: The same share it has of the population
explain: That single sentence is the whole method, and the calculation below is just it written as a fraction.

text: The idea: keep the shape of the population

md:
A sample is **stratified** when every group takes the same share of the sample as it has of the population. If one fifth of a club is under 12, one fifth of the sample is under 12.
That gives one rule, used over and over:
$\text{from a group} = \dfrac{\text{group size}}{\text{population}} \times \text{sample size}$

title: Why a share and not a count
md: A sample is meant to be the population in miniature. If juniors are a quarter of the club, a sample where they are a tenth would under-report whatever juniors think or do. Keeping each group's share fixed is the only way the smaller picture keeps the shape of the larger one.

prompt: A population of 800 contains a group of 200. How many of that group belong in a stratified sample of 40?
explain: 200 ÷ 800 × 40 = 10. The group is a quarter of the population, so a quarter of the sample.

md:
Two finishing habits turn three marks into four.
**Whole people.** A share of 16.2 is rounded to 16: you cannot sample a fifth of a person.
**Check the total.** Add your rounded numbers; they must come to the sample size. If four groups round to 49 when 50 were asked for, give the extra place to the group whose exact value had the largest decimal part — that is the group rounding treated worst.

prompt: A stratified calculation gives 13.75 members. What goes on the answer line?
explain: Round to the nearest whole member. A decimal number of people costs the accuracy mark.

prompt: A group of 250 in a population of 2000 contributes how many to a stratified sample of 48?
explain: 250 ÷ 2000 × 48 = 6. The group is one eighth of the population, so one eighth of the sample.

text: The hard version: sampling from a subgroup

md:
Read this sentence twice: **“A stratified sample of 30 is taken from those who waited longer than 20 minutes.”** The population for this calculation is no longer the whole table — it is that subgroup, and its total goes underneath the fraction.
With 24, 36, 48, 30 and 12 in the five classes, the subgroup is $48 + 30 + 12 = 90$. If the question then asks for those between 25 and 40 minutes, cut the classes: $\tfrac{5}{10} \times 48 = 24$ and $\tfrac{10}{20} \times 30 = 15$, giving 39. So the sample contains $\tfrac{39}{90} \times 30 = 13$.

prompt: A class is $20 < t \le 30$ with frequency 48. How many values lie between 25 and 30, assuming an even spread?
explain: 25 to 30 is 5 of the 10 minutes, so take half of 48.

text: Estimating a population you cannot count

md:
You cannot count the fish in a lake. So: catch some, mark them, put them back, wait, catch again, and see what fraction of the new catch is marked. If the marked fish have mixed back through the lake, that fraction is the fraction of the whole lake that is marked:
$\dfrac{\text{marked in the second catch}}{\text{size of the second catch}} = \dfrac{\text{number you marked}}{\text{population}}$
With 24 marked, then 4 marked in a catch of 30: $\tfrac{4}{30} = \tfrac{24}{N}$, so $N = \tfrac{24 \times 30}{4} = 180$ fish. **Whole fish**, and the word 'about' in front.

prompt: 40 squirrels are marked. Later 50 are caught and 8 are marked. Estimate the population.

title: Summer 2024 M4 Q15
md: Only about a quarter reached the estimate; **most did not recognise the proportion argument** at all. Some who did left a decimal number of animals. And the critique in part (b) was usually generic — 'the sample is too small' — when the marks were for faults in **the method described**: marks wearing off, animals not mixing back, births and deaths between the catches.

prompt: Which criticism of a capture-recapture study would earn a mark?
options: The marks may have worn off, so marked animals are recorded as unmarked
The sample is too small to be reliable
answer: The marks may have worn off, so marked animals are recorded as unmarked
explain: It names something in the method described. The other two could be said about any study at all.

text: When the question hands you numbers, calculate

md:
Some parts ask whether a sample is fair, or why an answer is only an estimate. These look like writing questions and are not.
If figures are given, the mark is for **using them**: find the proportion in the population, apply it to the sample, and compare. A club of 180 with 45 juniors is 25% junior, so a fair sample of 60 would hold 15 juniors; if it holds 9, the juniors are under-represented — and that sentence is the answer.
If the question asks why an answer is an estimate, name the **assumption**: the data is grouped, so values were assumed to be spread evenly inside a class.

prompt: A club of 180 members has 45 juniors. In a fair sample of 60, how many juniors would you expect?
explain: 45 ÷ 180 = 25%, and 25% of 60 is 15. That number is what you compare the sample against.

prompt: A town is 22% over 65; a sample of 200 contains 24 people over 65. Which comment earns the mark?
options: 22% of 200 is 44, but only 24 were asked, so the over-65s are under-represented
The sample is too small to be representative
answer: 22% of 200 is 44, but only 24 were asked, so the over-65s are under-represented
explain: One calculation with the numbers given, then a comparison. The other two are memorised and use nothing from the question.

prompt: On a histogram, how do you turn a bar into a frequency?
explain: The area of the bar is the frequency. Bar heights on their own cannot be added.

title: Sheet or memory?
md:
**On the Higher formula sheet:** nothing for this topic.
**Must be known:** group ÷ population × sample size; the recapture proportion, marked in sample over sample size equals marked in population over population; part of a class $= \dfrac{\text{part width}}{\text{class width}} \times$ frequency; frequency $=$ frequency density $\times$ class width.

prompt: You are stuck on a 3-mark stratified part. What is the first thing worth writing down?
options: The total of the group the sample is taken from
The answer you think is most likely
answer: The total of the group the sample is taken from
explain: That is the first method mark, and it is available before any answer appears.

md:
Take each group's share of the population as its share of the sample.
Narrow the population first when the question names a subgroup.
Cut a class in proportion to get part of it.
Round to whole people and check the parts add to the sample.
Estimate a population from a marked-and-recaptured sample.

**Estimate how many** or **Complete the table**, often with **show your working out clearly** printed underneath. The first mark is the fraction giving each group's share; the last is a whole number of people that adds to the sample size. Stuck: write the group total over the population total and multiply by the sample.
